articles.author: Chandelis Duster
articles.description: Berlin police said they have identified a suspect who "is known to police" and has links to "Islamist circles."
articles.title: One dead, several injured after vehicle plows through crowd at Berlin Pride event

articles.author: Chandelis Duster
articles.description: At least one person has died in a fire in Spain, according to officials.
articles.title: France and Spain fires force more than 200,000 to flee homes

articles.author: Nina Totenberg
articles.description: Former President Joe Biden is declining to appeal a court ruling that allows the Justice Department to publicize recordings of conversations between him and a writer collaborating on his memoir.
articles.title: Biden ghostwriter tapes to be released

articles.author: Diaa Hadid
articles.description: Led by Gen-Z youth across India, the movement has become perhaps the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his 12 years in office.
articles.title: India's 'cockroach' movement ousts minister, but can Modi calm youth?

articles.author: Malaka Gharib
articles.description: Back in the '90s, I learned the art of staying cool in Egypt. At that time, air conditioning was not common. In the extremely hot summer of 2026, how are people managing?
articles.title: COMIC: Temps are predicted to hit 106 in Egypt this week. How do people stay cool?

articles.author: Raul Roman
articles.description: Water is often a scarce commodity in Nairobi's largest slum. The only source may be a local cartel — and with that comes the risk of sexual threats and attacks.
articles.title: Some women who can't afford water are often pressured to provide sex for it

articles.author: Durrie Bouscaren
articles.description: As Nigeria grapples with a rapid rise in cancer cases, patients say they often feel as if they are on their own.
articles.title: Cancer rates are rising faster here than anywhere else. Are healthcare systems ready?

articles.author: Aisha Harris
articles.description: Ross McElwee's documentaries have always been personal. After his son died, he wondered if it was all worth it.
articles.title: 'Remake' will wreck you: A filmmaker faces his own family footage

articles.author: Rafael Nam
articles.description: Trump's determination to find new legal justifications for his tariffs threatens to prolong the uncertainty facing the U.S. and global economies.
articles.title: Trump is hellbent on tariffs. Here are 5 implications

articles.author: Elena Moore
articles.description: Democrats are hoping to move past Graham Platner's scandal-plagued campaign as they look to unseat Susan Collins. In Jackson, they chose a nominee with a similar economic populist message as Platner.
articles.title: Democrats in Maine formally nominate Troy Jackson as their new candidate for U.S. Senate

articles.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
articles.description:
Campaigners say existing federal ban on phone or video calls for assisted dying consultations adversely affects people living in regional Australia

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Labor will come under pressure to allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth services, with the Greens and independent Kate Chaney to introduce legislation based on changes to Labor’s national platform.
Last week’s national conference in Adelaide changed the ALP platform and committed Labor to overturn a Howard-era law banning people from having medical appointments regarding euthanasia via telehealth services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Albanese at odds with Labor policy which now says telehealth should be allowed for euthanasia consultations

articles.author: Deborah Cole in Berlin
articles.description:
Suspected ⁠perpetrator ⁠identified by police as member of ⁠city’s ‘Islamist scene’
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to punish those responsible after a car struck people on the outskirts of Berlin’s Gay Pride celebrations, killing at least one person and wounding 16 others.
A suspected ⁠perpetrator of the apparent attack on ⁠Saturday night has been ⁠identified as a member of the ⁠city’s “Islamist scene” but he ​has not ‌yet ‌been arrested, a Berlin police spokesperson said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin Pride

articles.author: Kevin Rawlinson and Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Scottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fire
Residents of Nethy Bridge have been told they can return to their homes after a large fire broke out in the Cairngorms national park.
Supt Judy Hill of Police Scotland said: “Thanks to the efforts of fire crews, gamekeepers, contractors, partners and many others over the past 24 hours, there is no longer the immediate threat which prompted the evacuation of properties in Nethy Bridge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Evacuated villagers in Cairngorms allowed home after wildfire threat lifts

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie
articles.description:
Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by the Metropolitan police.
The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by The Guardian

articles.author: Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
More than a million children across the US have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) food benefits since Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to a new report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP).
The analysis found that more than 4 millions Americans were removed from Snap from July 2025 to March 2026, marking a significant decline in participation in the federal food assistance program.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: More than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passed

articles.author: Oliver Milman and agencies
articles.description:
Temperatures of 95-105F (35-40C) are expected, spanning Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwest
About 70 million people in the US are set to face excessive heat advisories as dangerously hot temperatures scorch much of the country’s southern and central states.
The third major “heat dome” event to hit the US in the past month is gathering strength over the weekend, spanning a vast swathe of the country, from the Gulf of Mexico coast to the Great Plains and the midwest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scorching US heatwave to hit 70 million people with third ‘heat dome’ in month

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Vega made remarks to ABC’s John Quiñones at  National Association of Hispanic Journalists conference 
Cecilia Vega, the former 60 Minutes correspondent, said on Thursday she felt pressured by CBS News’s executives to incorporate “political bias” into segments for the broadcast program.
Vega made the remarks during an onstage interview with John Quiñones, the ABC News correspondent, at the National Association of Hispanic Journalists’ annual conference in New Orleans. Her comments were first reported by Status.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cecilia Vega of 60 Minutes says she felt pressure from CBS to add ‘political bias’

articles.author: Shrai Popat in Bangor, Maine
articles.description:
Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
In a race defined by scandal, withdrawals and a frantic hunt for a replacement candidate, Maine Democrats hit reset on their chaotic Senate primary on Saturday as Troy Jackson officially secured the party’s nomination.
He took the stage at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to rapturous applause, a standing ovation and Noah Kahan’s Northern Attitude blaring over the speakers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary race

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah, Taz Ali and Hamish Mackay
articles.description:
Meanwhile, in the UK, a blaze in the Cairngorms national park has been described as ‘very serious’ by Scotland’s first minister

Tell us: have you been affected by wildfires in Europe?

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has requested the armed forces to deploy an Airbus A400M military transport aircraft earlier than originally planned to help tackle the major wildfires in Gironde, according to Le Monde.
The French newspaper reported the aircraft’s use was not originally expected until the end of the month due to the technical preparations and tests required beforehand.
While the fires raging across forests in France are a dramatic reminder of three successive heatwaves in as many months, the state of the country’s rivers provides another, no less worrying insight into the impact of extreme heat supercharged by the climate crisis.
The Loire, France’s longest river, is at a historical low, with the flow of some branches, including through the city of Orléans, reduced to a trickle between sandbanks. Two weeks ago, 16% of French rivers were reported to have dried up. A quarter of small streams were stagnant or had disappeared altogether, according to the national low water observatory. There has been little rain since.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: France and Spain race to control wildfires as more than 250,000 evacuated – as it happened

articles.author: William Christou
articles.description:
Hundreds of firefighters battle blazes as strong winds drive fires towards Bordeaux and smoke prompts health warnings in Madrid 
Unrestrained wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 250,000 people to flee, authorities from both countries have said, as they struggle to contain the blazes.
About 70,000 people were evacuated from central Spain, while 197,000 people fled in France, including tens of thousands from the wine region city of Bordeaux.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: More than 250,000 people flee wildfires in France and Spain

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Production at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.
Andy Burnham’s new government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despite opposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea

articles.author: Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Firefighters responded to an emergency call and found the bodies, six of which were those of children
A devastating tragedy has unfolded in Michigan after emergency crews responding to a house fire found eight members of the same family, including six children, dead. At least some of the dead inside the home had gunshot wounds.
Deputies with the Ottawa county sheriff’s office and firefighters from the Grand Haven fire department were dispatched at about 11.40am local time on Friday to a residence on Riverside Trail in Grand Haven Township.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eight family members found dead in Michigan fire, some with gunshot wounds

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Dharmendra Pradhan steps down after demonstrations over exam leak scandal, prompting celebrations among thousands of protesters
India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has resigned after a week of mass demonstrations, handing a major victory to a new youth movement that has posed an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.
In a statement on Saturday afternoon, Pradhan said he had submitted his letter of resignation to the prime minister after student pressure.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests

articles.author: Amrit Dhillon in Delhi
articles.description:
Bollywood stars accused of ‘cowardice’ as hundreds of thousands of young Indians take to the streets to challenge government
Bollywood stars and other Indian celebrities have faced fierce criticism for staying silent in the face of some of the biggest protests India has seen in years.
Hundreds of thousands of young Indians took to the streets this week as part of a new youth movement that calls itself the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), demanding accountability over exam paper leaks in an unprecedented challenge to prime minister Narendra Modi’s government. Many vented their anger against what they saw as “cowardice” from India’s biggest celebrities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Indian celebrities fiercely criticised for silence on Cockroach protests

articles.author: William Christou
articles.description:
Saudi air defences intercept ballistic missiles as Iran reports first night without US strikes in two weeks
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week.
Iran, meanwhile, reported no strikes overnight on Saturday for the first time after two weeks of US attacks. The Iranian health ministry spokesperson, Hossein Kermanpour, said: “Iran had a peaceful night” in a post on X. Tensions, however, remain high.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis claim missile attack on Saudi Arabia as regional tensions escalate

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Jewellery made from BC Iran worn at Odyssey photocall throws spotlight on the trade of rare archeological finds
The Odyssey has stormed cinemas, but while its take on the Homeric epic has created ripples among western classicists, it is an actor’s earrings that have made waves further afield.
Zendaya, who portrays the goddess Athena in the movie, provoked outrage when she appeared at a London photocall wearing earrings that were allegedly made from Iranian artefacts dating back to the 1st millennium BC.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Treasure as trinkets: Zendaya’s earrings renew debate on ownership of ancient artefacts

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
articles.description:
Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
The lawyer for the families of Axel Rudakubana’s victims has said the Southport killer is “trying to retraumatise the families from his cell” after it emerged he had been transferred from prison to a psychiatric hospital.
Rudakubana, now 19, was given a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Southport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyer

articles.author: James Risen
articles.description:
After a Kyiv visit, rightwing firebrand now supports Ukraine – but perhaps it’s just because Trump favors a winner
Laura Loomer, the online Maga provocateur, has never worked in the White House or anywhere else in the government, but her sudden conversion to the Ukrainian cause this week is significant because her social media posts often have real policy implications in the second Trump administration.
The rightwing commentator has spent the last few days in Kyiv, where she announced a newfound sympathy for Ukraine in its long war with Russia, and admitted that she had previously fallen for Russian propaganda.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What’s behind Maga influencer Laura Loomer’s about-face on Ukraine?

articles.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
articles.description:
Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Lucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. Life could hardly get any better. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,” said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England.
That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the case

articles.author: Kaamil Ahmed
articles.description:
‘I can’t tolerate this life,’ said the 24-year-old in his last voice message to his relatives. Attacked by the military, a rebel army and criminal gangs, Siraz Ullah risked all for a better future
The fear was audible as he spoke, recording a message to his family, asking for their prayers. After pressing send, 24-year-old Siraz Ullah boarded a boat he hoped could deliver him from the violence and persecution surrounding him at home in Myanmar.
Instead, Siraz is among 500 Rohingya refugees who have vanished at sea after setting sail for Malaysia in late June.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Family of missing Rohingya footballer fear he is among 500 believed dead in Myanmar shipwrecks

articles.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem; photographs by Amjed Tantesh
articles.description:
In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives
Swimming classes have started again in Gaza after three years of war, with hundreds of children learning to float, doggy paddle and take their first strokes in five makeshift sea pools built from sandbags and rubble.
The lessons allow a few hundred girls and boys to reclaim their childhood for a few hours in a place where there are no playgrounds, no formal education and children live in fear of continuing Israeli attacks. A UN survey in March found that 96% of children felt death was imminent.
Activity on the Gaza seafront
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Reclaiming stolen childhoods: swimming classes resume in Gaza after three years of war

articles.author: Andrew Messenger
articles.description:
Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Syngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.
The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemical announced by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in June.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Herbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical maker

articles.author: Helena Smith in Litochoro
articles.description:
Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation
More than four decades have elapsed since Evangelos Geroliolios made his first ascent to the home of the ancient gods. At the top of Mount Olympus, on the rocky peak of Greece’s highest mountain, he felt unalloyed awe.
“I’ve never forgotten that unique moment, that unique feeling up there on the throne of Zeus,” recalled Geroliolios, who as mayor of Dion-Olympus now spends a great deal of his time administering the area around the site.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No time to waste’: Greece bids for Mount Olympus to be included on Unesco list of world heritage sites

articles.author: Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
President flew to Ankara onboard Qatari-gifted jet, without advanced defenses, and flew home on old Air Force One
Donald Trump switched aircraft before departing Turkey earlier this month after US officials determined there was a credible threat from Iranian proxy forces targeting him and Air Force One, according to a new report from the New York Times.
The threat surfaced while the US president was attending the Nato summit. He had arrived in Ankara onboard the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8, an aircraft that Trump acknowledged does not have the same advanced defensive systems as the older Air Force One.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump switched planes in Turkey earlier this month because of threat from Iran proxy forces – report

articles.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
The US has struck targets across Iran, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea, as Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the war to a second shipping ⁠chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.
As Iran retaliated on Friday with missile and drone fire against US bases and allies across the region, the New York Times reported that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire proposal delivered by the Iraq prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi. This despite the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claiming a day earlier that Iran was begging for a ceasefire. Iraq later disputed the report.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikes

articles.author: Reuters in Toronto
articles.description:
At least 90 active blazes in British Columbia in what PM says is one of the country’s most intense seasons on record

How dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?

Fresh wildfires have broken out in western Canada and forests continued to ⁠burn in Ontario as the country ⁠battled what the prime ​minister, Mark Carney, called one of the most intense wildfire seasons on record.
Nearly 34,000 lightning strikes over the past week led to a series of fires ⁠and evacuation orders in southern British Columbia. There were 25 evacuation orders and 90 active wildfires in the province as of Friday morning, and authorities said warming ⁠and drying conditions could cause them to grow.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thousands of lightning strikes trigger fresh wildfires in western Canada

articles.author: Associated Press in Georgetown
articles.description:
Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodies
The confirmed death toll from the recent capsizing of a state ferry off Guyana’s coast has risen to 72, with more bodies recovered as a multinational team struggle to salvage the partially submerged vessel.
Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 people were rescued. The government has estimated that 100 may have died in the accident, which would make it the worst marine tragedy on record for the South American nation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Guyanese authorities confirm death of 72 people in sinking of coastal ferry

articles.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
articles.description:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.
Financial markets now see an even chance the RBA board will deliver a fourth cash rate increase at the next meeting on 11 August.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australian households face prospect of interest rate hike and petrol prices rising above $2 a litre

articles.author: Ben Smee
articles.description:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence 

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

For a decade, Pauline Hanson has been beating the same drum.
Her comments this week – suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street” and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and been labelled “dangerous” by experts and other commentators.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumble

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall
The Cockroach activist Sonam Wangchuk has ended a 26-day hunger strike, as youth-led protests continued to erupt across India and leaders of the movement said there was no breakthrough in talks with the government.
Wangchuk had been fasting since June in solidarity with the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), a new youth-led movement that has been holding mass protests calling for government accountability and the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over exam paper leaks. The leaks affected 2 million students in May and have been linked to more than a dozen suicides.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Indian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spread

articles.author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
articles.description:
US agency is to pay Canadian media company US$125m for use of investigative database to detect ‘immigration fraud’
A Canadian federal opposition party leader has called on Mark Carney’s government to block the latest data-sharing deal between US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Canadian media company Thomson Reuters.
Avi Lewis, the federal leader of the New Democratic party (NDP), demanded on Tuesday that Ottawa address the contract and further restrict Canadian corporations from doing business with ICE, after Canada’s National Observer news website reported on the deal.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canadian government urged to block Thomson Reuters data deal with US ICE

articles.author: Jonathan Watts
articles.description:
Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon
Indigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.
Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Masked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leaders

articles.author: Caitlin Cassidy
articles.description:
Inquiry’s focus this week is on security for the Jewish community, with the MP telling the commissioner his son is afraid to attend synagogues and events

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, has called for universities to undertake an audit of any classes that teach about the Jewish community, Israel or Palestine.
Appearing before the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion on Friday, Leeser said he had been “very concerned” about antisemitism on university campuses and was not satisfied with how vice-chancellors had addressed the issue after the 7 October 2023 Hamas terrorist attack.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: University courses covering Israel-Palestine should be audited, Julian Leeser tells royal commission

articles.author: James Michelin for MetDesk
articles.description:
Fires remain out of control in Northwest Territories and Ontario, while Argentina endures record night-time heat
Recent hot, dry weather in Canada has triggered hundreds of wildfires across the country. As of Wednesday, more than 900 were burning, scorching about 3m hectares of land. While fires have broken out in several provinces, the greatest concern is in the Northwest Territories and Ontario, where several remain out of control.
Poor air quality has been reported across affected regions, with wildfire smoke carried by winds into the US and even across the Atlantic to northern Europe. The risk of further blazes remains high as North America enters the peak of fire season.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across Canada

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Hannah Ellis-Petersen; produced by Saskia Collette, Alex Atack and Brian McNamara; executive producer Eli Block
articles.description:
South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen on the Cockroach movement – and the students driving India’s biggest protests in years
‘I’ve never seen this many young people out on the streets,’ says Hannah Ellis-Petersen.
For days, tens of thousands of Indians have been marching under the banner of the Cockroach Janta party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The ‘cockroaches’ marching on India’s government – podcast

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
articles.description:
The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.
Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying

articles.author: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent
articles.description:
September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.
While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
articles.description:
Dunedin will be the focal point, having last experienced such an eclipse in 1163 – before any humans reached New Zealand
Hotels are booking out two years in advance in the New Zealand city of Dunedin as it prepares for the region’s first total solar eclipse in more than 850 years.
At 4.17pm on 22 July 2028, the moon will pass in front of the sun, casting a roughly 100km-wide shadowy band across parts of southern New Zealand. Everywhere within that band – from tourist hotspot Queenstown in the west to Dunedin city in the east – will be plunged into daytime darkness for 2 minutes and 51 seconds.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Total solar eclipse books out hotels two years in advance in New Zealand city

articles.author: Danny Vincent
articles.description:
Isabel Rose, 26, sentenced to six years for blackmail and perverting course of public justice over her allegations against British man
A British woman who reported being raped to police in Hong Kong has been sentenced to six years in prison for blackmail and perverting the course of public justice.
Isabel Rose, 26, from south-east London, travelled to Hong Kong in early 2024 to visit a British banker she had met while travelling in south-east Asia.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British woman jailed in Hong Kong for blackmail after accusing banker of rape

articles.author: Sarah Basford Canales and Luca Ittimani
articles.description:
Foreign minister Penny Wong will deliver speech criticising China’s recent launch of a nuclear-capable submarine-launched missile

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Penny Wong will warn China that Australia and other neighbouring nations will not be bullied by its “provocative” actions, after its involvement in another “destabilising and dangerous” incident this week.
The foreign affairs minister – who will deliver the address on Thursday in the Philippines, where the 59th Asean foreign minister’s meeting is being held – will also caution world leaders against placing a toll on the strait of Hormuz after both Iran and the US threatened to do amid the protracted conflict.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia to warn China it won’t be bullied by ‘provocative‘ actions as it builds military and nuclear arsenal

articles.author: Raphael Rashid
articles.description:
Prosecutors seek a one-year sentence and heavy fine after chef garnished dish with insects not approved for consumption
Prosecutors in South Korea have asked a court to sentence the owner of a Michelin-starred restaurant to one year in prison for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.
The request, made on Monday, also sought a 20m won (£10,108) fine for the company that runs the restaurant, Yonhap news agency reported.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Michelin-starred restaurant owner in South Korea faces jail over ant dessert

articles.author: Gavin Blair in Tokyo
articles.description:
In April Japan coined new term kokushobi for days above 40C as country advises workers to wear shorts to the office to cope with stifling heat
Japan logged its first official kokushobi or “cruelly hot day” on Tuesday since the new term for when temperatures top 40 degrees Celsius was introduced in April. The Japan Meteorological Agency coined the new designation to warn the public of the heat dangers of days that were once freak weather events but have now become more common.
The central Japan cities of Gujo and Tajimi in Gifu prefecture, along with Toyota in Aichi prefecture, all hit 40C. Gujo’s 40C and Toyota’s 40.1C were all-time highs recorded at their respective weather stations.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan records its first ‘cruelly hot day’ as cities swelter in 40-degree heat

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.
The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC

articles.author: Kat Lay Global health correspondent
articles.description:
Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy as report shows 2.69bn people can’t afford to eat well
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.
There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds

articles.author: Eromo Egbejule in Abidjan
articles.description:
Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.
According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Judge rejects administration’s request to lift injunction secured by several Democratic-led states on 25 June
A federal appeals court on Saturday declined to allow Donald Trump’s administration to implement in 23 states his executive order that aims to tighten rules for mail-in voting before the November elections that ⁠will decide control of Congress.
The Boston-based ⁠first US circuit court ​of appeals rejected the administration’s request to lift an injunction several Democratic-led states secured on 25 June from a lower-court judge who concluded that key parts of the Republican president’s order were unconstitutional. In asking the court to ⁠pause the US district judge Indira Talwani’s ruling while it pursues an appeal, the Department of Justice argued that because government agencies had yet to finalize actions and policies to implement Trump’s directive, any lawsuit challenging his order was premature.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Appeals court rejects Trump bid to curb mail-in voting in 23 states

articles.author: Marina Dunbar
articles.description:
Analysis finds more than 4 million Americans lost Snap benefits, or food stamps, from July 2025 to March 2026
More than a million children across the US have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) food benefits since Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to a new report from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP).
The analysis found that more than 4 millions Americans were removed from Snap from July 2025 to March 2026, marking a significant decline in participation in the federal food assistance program.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: More than 1 million children lost access to food benefits after Trump bill passed

articles.author: Shrai Popat in Bangor, Maine
articles.description:
Progressive former state senate president gains nomination after Graham Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations
In a race defined by scandal, withdrawals and a frantic hunt for a replacement candidate, Maine Democrats hit reset on their chaotic Senate primary on Saturday as Troy Jackson officially secured the party’s nomination.
He took the stage at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor to rapturous applause, a standing ovation and Noah Kahan’s Northern Attitude blaring over the speakers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate seat after chaotic primary race

articles.author: Oliver Milman
articles.description:
Frank Yiannas calls for an independent review of the federal response to the illness causing explosive diarrhea
Donald Trump’s former top food safety official has accused the administration of a near “catastrophic” mismanagement of the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands of people in the US.
There should be an independent review of the federal government’s response to the rash of illnesses caused by the spread of a parasite found on raw produce, according to Frank Yiannas, who was deputy commissioner for food policy at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) across the presidencies of both Trump and Joe Biden from 2018 to 2023.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Former FDA official says US handling of cyclospora near ‘catastrophic level’

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Jackson, a prominent workers’ rights advocate and a leading progressive voice, replaces the scandal-plagued Graham Platner
As cinemagoers flock to The Odyssey, Democrats in Maine are hoping that their long and perilous quest for a political hero ends in Troy.
They have nominated lumberjack Troy Jackson this weekend as their candidate to challenge Susan Collins, a veteran Republican in the US Senate, after the implosion of the party’s original candidate left them scrambling for a replacement less than four months before the midterm elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Troy Jackson: the Maine lumberjack Democrats believe can beat Susan Collins

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
A new report shows more Senate-confirmed staffers have left their jobs this time around than in his first term
Donald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates.
According to a new report called Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’s nearly 150% higher than the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Douglas Main in Tucson, Arizona
articles.description:
Environmental groups are sounding the alarm over plans that threaten a desert spring that’s home to rare fish and turtles and sacred to the O’odham people
Quitobaquito Springs in south-west Arizona has been called a biological wonderland with few equals.
The springs are an oasis in the vast Sonoran desert along the US-Mexico border, held sacred by the O’odham people, who call it A’al Vaipia. Here, water flows out of an aquifer at the bottom of a hill, runs along a short concrete channel and collects in a pond.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: This desert oasis is a biological wonderland. Trump’s border wall threatens to destroy it

articles.author: Eduardo Porter
articles.description:
Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all

US politics live – latest updates

Don’t believe the Trump administration’s rationale for its new volley of tariffs against everybody.
The new levies, ostensibly to punish countries for failing to do enough to curb forced labor, switched on at 12.01am on Friday, to coincide with the expiration of a temporary 10% blanket duty that Donald Trump imposed in February, ostensibly to protect the United States from a balance-of-payments crisis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo Porter

articles.author: Lateefah Simon and Guillermo Mayer
articles.description:
The US will no longer hold transportation agencies accountable for unintentional discrimination. That’s devastating for those of us who depend on it
As the first congenitally blind member of Congress and a former president of the Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) board, I know that the ability to move – to get to work, to school, to the doctor – is a freedom our nation’s civil rights laws have long promised to protect. Last month, the Trump administration derailed that promise.
Through a regulatory maneuver designed to evade public scrutiny, the Department of Transportation announced it will no longer hold transportation agencies accountable when their decisions produce discriminatory outcomes – no matter how severe – so long as the discrimination was unintentional. As a result, decades of civil rights protection were erased by regulatory fiat.
Congresswoman Lateefah Simon represents California’s 12th congressional district in the East Bay. She is the first congenitally blind member to serve in Congress and a strong advocate for transportation and disability justice. She previously served as Bart president and executive director of the San Francisco Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights
Guillermo Mayer is an attorney and the president and CEO of Public Advocates, a 55-year old civil rights law firm and advocacy organization dedicated to challenging the systemic causes of poverty and racial discrimination
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Public transit is a lifeline for countless Americans. Trump is derailing our protections | Lateefah Simon and Guillermo Mayer

articles.author: Steve Bloomfield
articles.description:
The US is aligning itself with dictators and autocrats to prevent those accused of genocide, ethnic cleansing and war crimes from ever facing justice
Barely a month appears to go by without Donald Trump making a fresh attempt to destroy the international rules-based order. The US has pulled funding from dozens of international institutions, shut down USAID and withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement. Nato may survive on paper, but Trump has made clear that he has little interest in coming to the aid of any ally that is attacked. The Board of Peace is clearly an attempt to sideline the United Nations.
But the state department’s announcement last week that it wishes to dismantle the international criminal court “brick by brick” could be Trump’s most frightening move of all.
Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump says he will dismantle the ICC ‘brick by brick’. It could be his most chilling move of all | Steve Bloomfield

articles.author: Guardian staff
articles.description:
Late-night host discussed Trump’s claims of a rigged 2020 election, push for voting changes and new Canadian tariffs
Last night, Seth Meyers focused on Donald Trump’s claims that China swayed the 2020 election, new tariffs on Canadian imports and his attempt to impose voting restrictions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s approval ratings: ‘Worse than Bush during the Iraq war’

articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
articles.description:
People have found language for moodiest part of their menstrual cycles, and the right has seized on it
Emily Rae Detrick, a health coach, wants women to be more in touch with their menstrual cycle in its entirety. This, she said on an October episode of Culture Apothecary with Alex Clark, a podcast popular among “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) adherents, is “a way that you honor God and the way we were created”. It also serves her self-assigned mission to help “make America fertile again”.
In the episode and on social media, Detrick speaks at length about the luteal phase, the 14-ish days between ovulation and menstruation when women are more likely to experience irritability, bloating and food cravings. If a woman does not get pregnant after ovulating, or so Detrick’s line of thinking goes, her body becomes upset. “During the luteal phase, the reason why your stress threshold is so much lower is because this is the time your body would be incubating a potential baby,” she said. No baby, and you might turn into a frazzled, nagging shrew.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Why do I feel crappy?’: women are learning about their luteal phases - and Maha is weaponizing it

articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.description:
Anton Jäger has been lauded for his exceptional ability to make sense of these strange political times – and he’s only 32. The writer and academic explains why we’re living in an age of hyperpolitics
‘I am acutely conscious,” said Andy Burnham outside 10 Downing Street on Monday, “that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street.” It was good to hear him say it because, beneath all the cabinet gossip and rune-reading, there is a feeling of terror about the immediate future and also about ourselves, the electorate. Is this who we are now? Wildly enthusiastic one minute, seething the next; as passionate about the change we want as we are convinced that those who promise it are incapable of enacting it?
It is perhaps not surprising that Anton Jäger’s recent book, Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization without Political Consequences, is being read by Labour watchers and leftwing thinkers. As the New York Times wrote, it’s “among the best and most dazzling efforts to model the political present in all its maddening strangeness”. Still, I think Jäger was surprised to have his honeymoon interrupted so I could interview him about it. Life comes at everyone quite fast in a hyperpolitical age.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Meet the man whose groundbreaking book is being devoured by the left

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman , with David Smith and Rachel Leingang . Produced by Suzanne Gaber and Tiara Chiaramonte , edited by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev
articles.description:
Earlier this year, Congress reached a depressing milestone: 86% of Americans, a record high, disapproved of its job performance. But this summer, there have been some signs that shifts are underway. On the left, House Democrats have just voted in unprecedented numbers to withhold military aid from Israel, and across the country, progressive candidates are running competitive primary campaigns that are energizing a base fed up with the status quo. On the right, Republicans are reeling from the sudden death of Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator and one of Donald Trump's staunchest supporters. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, remains sequestered following a health scare in June, raising questions of if a changing of the guard might be underway there, too. Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by David Smith, the Guardian's Washington bureau chief and Rachel Leingang, midwest political correspondent, to discuss gerontocracy, transparency, the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and just how much of an inflection point this summer might be for both parties


This page was amended on 23 July 2026. A previous version misspelled Lindsey Graham. 

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is US Congress finally on the verge of a change? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Sam Levine Zhara Keogh Michael Kalenderian Sarah Bertram
articles.description:
Donald Trump delivered a primetime address to the country on Thursday, claiming that declassified intelligence showed Chinese interference in US elections. The US president revived long-running attacks on election security, despite a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which he lost. The Guardian's voting rights reporter Sam Levine factchecks some of Trump's claims

Trump is invoking foreign election interference to justify his own - Opinion

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fact-checking Donald Trump’s address on Chinese election interference – video

articles.author: Hosted by Jonathan Freedland . Produced by May Robson, Jacob Liebenberg, Ned Carter Miles and the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj .
articles.description:
The debate about how old is too old to serve in public office has resurfaced this week after the shock death of the Republican senator Lindsey Graham and the surprise return of Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old senator who published a photo of himself in hospital after a long absence from the spotlight.
With rumours continuing to swirl around Donald Trump’s health, why is it US politicians seem to cling on to power for so long?
Jonathan Freedland speaks to Alexis Coe, a presidential historian and columnist for the New York Times Book review, about whether the US is becoming a gerontocracy – and what can be done about it
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are American politicians too old? | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman , with Shrai Popat and Lauren Gambino . Produced by Meg Driscoll, edited by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev
articles.description:
Earlier this week, Graham Platner, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Maine, was accused by a former partner of sexual assault. Platner denies the allegations, but on Wednesday, he suspended his campaign, accusing the “political establishment” of tanking his candidacy. But this is only the most recent scandal to have surfaced around Platner’s campaign — over the past year, the oyster farmer and combat veteran was revealed to have a tattoo that closely resembled a Totenkopf (a widely recognized Nazi symbol), a long paper trail of racist, misogynist and homophobic posts on Reddit, and in June, the New York Times published allegations from three former partners about Platner’s “toxic” behavior in their relationships, including, in several cases, physical intimidation (allegations Platner denied).
As Democrats regroup and evaluate their dwindling chances to flip the Senate in November, hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by Guardian political reporters Lauren Gambino and Shrai Popat to ask why voters flocked to Platner, why they were reluctant to abandon him as the scandals came out — and what the whole mess says about who gets the privilege of political redemption.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why Graham Platner wasn’t the answer to the Democrats’ man problem – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Kevin Rawlinson and Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Scottish first minister thanks Nethy Bridge residents and aid workers after earlier requesting UK military aid to fight 10-day fire
Residents of Nethy Bridge have been told they can return to their homes after a large fire broke out in the Cairngorms national park.
Supt Judy Hill of Police Scotland said: “Thanks to the efforts of fire crews, gamekeepers, contractors, partners and many others over the past 24 hours, there is no longer the immediate threat which prompted the evacuation of properties in Nethy Bridge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Evacuated villagers in Cairngorms allowed home after wildfire threat lifts

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie
articles.description:
Scotland Yard is looking at two £250,000 donations to the party by Britain Means Business before the 2024 election
Payments to Reform UK first revealed by the Guardian are now being investigated by the Metropolitan police.
The inquiry is scrutinising payments made to the party via a company controlled by its deputy leader, Richard Tice.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police investigate payments to Reform UK first revealed by The Guardian

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Blunder at Rosebank, UK’s biggest undeveloped oilfield, comes as government considers granting licence
Production at Britain’s biggest undeveloped oil and gasfield could be delayed for months after equipment from a rig was accidentally dropped in the North Sea, the Guardian can reveal.
Andy Burnham’s new government is under pressure from the fossil fuel industry to allow oil to be retrieved from the Rosebank site despite opposition from climate campaigners and some Labour MPs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New North Sea oil drilling faces delay after gear accidentally dropped in sea

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
Sanae Takaichi’s blueprint to inject £1.7tn and double economic growth leaves many investors fearful
International investors are asking where Japan’s prime minister will find the ¥370tn (£1.7tn) of extra cash that she wants to invest in 17 industrial sectors by 2040.
Such is the scale of spending by Sanae Takaichi’s coalition government that many in her own party fear she is about to blow up the Japanese economy, triggering a Liz Truss-style economic shock.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Japan avoid a Liz Truss-style shock as its PM embarks on a giant spending spree?

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Trump administration has clashed with Vatican on social issues but Burnham’s faith is shaped by different principles 
With the appointment of Britain’s first lifelong Roman Catholic prime minister, the faith is now in a prominent political position on both sides of the Atlantic.
But while Donald Trump’s administration, in particular the vice-president, JD Vance – a Catholic convert – has placed Catholicism at the heart of its culture wars and repeatedly clashed with the Vatican over the US’s hardline stance on social issues, Andy Burnham has been shaped by a British Catholic tradition with a different set of political priorities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The UK has its first Catholic PM – but don’t expect a US-style religious culture war to follow

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
articles.description:
Comment follows news Axel Rudakubana was transferred from prison to psychiatric hospital
The lawyer for the families of Axel Rudakubana’s victims has said the Southport killer is “trying to retraumatise the families from his cell” after it emerged he had been transferred from prison to a psychiatric hospital.
Rudakubana, now 19, was given a life sentence for the murders of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Southport killer ‘trying to retraumatise families from cell’, says lawyer

articles.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
articles.description:
Eighteen months after her daughter’s death in Texas, Jane Coates hopes new PM can persuade US authorities to reopen case
Lucy Harrison felt that 2024 was her best year yet. The 23-year-old had graduated from university with first class honours, landed her dream job and bought her first house with her boyfriend. She was a “big girl adult” now, Lucy would say. She shed tears of joy seeing her idol, Taylor Swift, at Wembley on the Eras tour that summer. Life could hardly get any better. “All the hard work, all the tears, everything was coming to fruition,” said her mother, Jane Coates, from Warrington in north-west England.
That Christmas, Lucy and her boyfriend, Sam Littler, flew to Texas to spend time with her father, Kris Harrison, who had left the family home when she was two. The pair had a complex relationship – Harrison was a recovering alcoholic – and Littler, 24, did not want them to go. But Lucy enjoyed seeing her two younger half-sisters at their home in Prosper, an affluent suburb 30 miles north of Dallas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lucy Harrison’s father was holding the gun that killed her but was never arrested. Now her mother wants Andy Burnham to take up the case

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Officials not satisfied Therese Abdallah is a ‘genuine visitor’ and believe she would not leave after visit to son in London
A Palestinian Jerusalemite who lives in London has been left devastated after a planned trip by his parents had to be cancelled when the Home Office ruled his mother was not a “genuine visitor” but granted his father a visa.
Karim Abdallah, who has lived in the UK since 2019, was looking forward to hosting his parents, Therese Abdallah, 69, a retired English teacher, and his father, Ghassan Abdallah, a psychologist, for a few weeks.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Home Office rejects Palestinian Jerusalemite woman’s UK visa but approves husband’s

articles.author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
articles.description:
Campaigners urge government to introduce right of access to water, particularly as heatwaves become more common
Almost three-quarters of riverbanks in England have no public access, according to data released by the Right to Roam campaign.
Across the country, the public cannot use riverbanks or gain access to the rivers themselves in most of the river catchments from the west of Cornwall up to the Tweed, which flows through northern England and Scotland.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Almost 75% of England’s riverbanks ‘off limits’ to public, figures show

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Research into GLP-1 medications is not always robust but complaints such as digestive problems are well known
Weight loss jabs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have boomed in popularity, and so have reports of myriad side-effects. This week researchers have suggested GLP-1 medications could be associated with hair loss.
It can be hard to keep tabs on which of these unintentional outcomes have been the subject of expert scrutiny and which remain little more than hearsay. We take a look at some of the most talked about side-effects and explore which have been studied – and which remain unproven.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Ozempic face’ and hair loss: what evidence is there for weight-loss drug side-effects?

articles.author: Priya Bharadia
articles.description:
From Mo Farah to Bus Aunty, new prime minister makes good on promise to ‘do things differently’ when it comes to communication
They say a week is a long time in politics, but handily for followers of Andy Burnham on social media, you can get daily updates of what the new PM has been up to on his timeline.
Before Burnham stepped inside No 10 this week he promised to “do things differently” in British politics. If his feed is anything to go by, he’s already way ahead of his predecessor.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The UK’s first TikTok PM? Andy Burnham channels Zohran Mamdani as he hits social media

articles.author: Richard Partington
articles.description:
In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century
The Cherry Tree pub is an unassuming local. On a busy road in the Cheshire village of Culcheth, it is a chain-run pub where four shots cost £8, every burger comes with a soft drink, and sport is shown all day on the big screens. It is also a favourite of Andy Burnham, the new prime minister.
Many of the drinkers have a story about – arguably – Culcheth’s most famous son.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: I grew up near Andy Burnham. This is what shaped the UK’s new PM

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Jalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authorities
Security has been increased by several hundred additional staff at the UK’s largest Muslim convention, Jalsa Salana, alongside enhanced coordination with police, emergency services and local authorities, against a backdrop of growing anti-Muslim sentiment.
Last month, another big Islamic gathering was forced to close early after 12 people were arrested, including three on suspicion of conspiracy to murder, over a suspected far-right threat.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK’s largest Muslim event goes ahead with added security as hate crime rises

articles.author: Rupert Jones
articles.description:
Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts say
It is shaping up to be a decent summer for savers as fierce competition among providers pushes up interest rates and increases choice.
You can currently get instant- and easy-access accounts that pay up to 5% interest, and fixed-rate savings bonds that pay almost that much. Meanwhile, those looking for a regular savings account can now get up to 8%.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK savings deals: the heat is on as banks offer up to 8%

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll in Donegal and agencies
articles.description:
Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicans 
A 25-year-old law student has been charged in relation to an “extremely significant” bomb intercepted near the UK-Irish border.
Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives at a special sitting of Trim district court on Friday evening.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Law student charged after military-grade bomb intercepted near Irish border

articles.author: Kiran Stacey and Patrick Butler
articles.description:
Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector
Hundreds of thousands of care workers could be exempted from the home secretary’s plans to toughen up the immigration system under proposals being considered by Andy Burnham as he looks for ways to relieve pressure on the social care sector.
The prime minister will give a speech next week spelling out his determination to start creating a National Care Service before the next general election as he looks to accelerate the process set up by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Existing care workers could be exempt from UK’s tough new immigration rules

articles.author: Amelia Hill
articles.description:
Business owners in England say prioritising venues selling alcohol leaves vital community spaces behind 
Ferdinand Geus is proud of the positive, global impact his small speciality coffee business is having.
“Around 3,000 small, family-owned farms in Yemen rely on us – we’ve persuaded many to stop growing khat, the drug, and start growing coffee instead,” said the business manager of Sheba Coffee, which supplies Yemeni coffee beans to independent cafes across the world, including the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s not fair’: cafe owners frustrated over exclusion from business rates cut

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
Exclusive: Eight companies expect to be covered by the ban for 2025-26, the Guardian can reveal
Water company bosses’ total pay rose over the past year despite a government bonus ban and public outrage over pollution and bills, the Guardian can reveal.
One chief executive, Mark Thurston of Anglian Water, received £1.9m – including a £500,000 “retention payment”, despite the bonus ban.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Water bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollution

articles.author: Hayden Vernon and agency
articles.description:
Warning in place until Sunday morning in southern and central regions after drought declared in parts of Wales
Heat alerts are in place across parts of England, with possible highs of 30C (86F) and officials saying temperatures are likely to have an impact on health and wellbeing.
The yellow heat health alerts issued for the East Midlands, east of England, London, south-east, south-west and West Midlands are in place until 9am on Sunday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parts of England under heat alert with 30C temperatures possible

articles.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
articles.description:
A physio, a tailor and a historian on the style trends that can put women in hospital and how to avoid the dangers
“Buyer beware” is one of the oldest principles in English law. Now, a pair of wide legged trousers from Zara is bringing the phrase back to the forefront of shoppers’ minds.
On social media the £25.99 wide-legged trousers from the high-street retailer have earned the moniker “Zara death pants” thanks to a slew of videos showing wearers tripping over the leg of the trousers and injuring themselves.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: From high heels to ‘Zara death pants’: how fashion falls foul of women’s safety

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Streaming pioneer that transformed TV faces slowing growth and battle for viewers’ attention from YouTube
When Netflix offered viewers the chance to binge on an entire season of House of Cards it revolutionised the TV industry and started on a path to becoming the world’s most popular streaming service.
Almost 15 years on, however, the upstart’s strategy of pumping its service with an avalanche of content and an almost-as-rapid penchant for mercilessly cancelling shows has viewers reaching for the remote.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Netflix has to evolve’: can the upstart survive the end of the binge-watch era?

articles.description:
The prime minister opened a new government base in Manchester, called No 10 North, intended to signal a shift away from what he said had been decades of economic decision-making centred in London. Heron House is temporarily accommodating No 10 North while a brownfield site just outside the city is being developed where it is expected to relocate permanently

UK politics live – latest updates

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham opens No 10 North in Manchester – video

articles.author: Lucy Swan, Kiran Stacey, Carmen Aguilar García and Heidi Wilson
articles.description:
Women have half the seats at the top table for the first time, but Oxbridge maintains its grip
Andy Burnham has appointed the first cabinet of his premiership. Much has been made of how key allies of his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have been demoted or sacked, but what is the demographic makeup of the new team of senior ministers, and how does it differ from other governments?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Race, school, gender: the makeup of Andy Burnham’s cabinet – in charts

articles.author: Gary Fuller
articles.description:
Team in Ohio finds swapping to electric has ‘very large’ impact, despite study being scaled back by Trump cuts
A US study has found a 70% drop in hospital admissions and days off from work or school when people with poorly controlled asthma had their gas stove and hob replaced with electric.
Ohio’s publicly owned MetroHealth began the study in December 2024 but funding was terminated early by the incoming Trump administration. It had been designed to investigate if replacing gas cooking improved asthma for 1,200 people living near Cleveland, Ohio.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Replacing gas stove can help asthmatics as much as some drugs, US experts find

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Writing from year after gross indecency arrest challenges ‘isolated mathematician’ image, says Cambridge academic
When people think of Alan Turing, they might imagine he was arrogant, isolated, humourless, tortured. A better way of remembering the father of modern computing would be, an academic argues, as “playful, funny, cheeky, literary, and someone who really liked sex”.
The Cambridge University English literature professor Sarah Dillon has transcribed and studied a little-known short story that Turing wrote in the year after his arrest in Manchester for gross indecency.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Racy short story by Alan Turing offers glimpse of ‘playful, funny, cheeky’ side

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
Black-crowned night heron one of many species thriving at Holnicote Estate where river ‘reset’ has transformed area into lush oasis
A rare black-crowned night heron has been spotted on an estate in the south-west of England where an innovative river “reset” is transforming the area into an oasis for birdlife.
The heron was caught on camera in a jungly corner of the Holnicote Estate, where conservation experts have been restoring the landscape by allowing a river to return to its natural course.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rare heron seen at Somerset estate where river has been allowed to run free

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Conservative leader is becoming more confident and forging a message for her party, but faces a new opponent 
“So, Andy Burnham seems like a nice guy.” Those were the slightly unexpected opening words of Kemi Badenoch’s first speech since the change in prime minister. But make no mistake: she was there to bury her opponent.
Even Badenoch-sceptics inside the Conservative party and farther afield agree the Tory leader is becoming more confident, and has been able to forge an increasingly coherent message for her party, one based on a promise of economic competence.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kemi Badenoch ‘has to adapt’ her rhetoric to take on Andy Burnham

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Escalating Houthi warnings to ships carrying Saudi crude through the strait lead to fears of further price surge
A fresh front in the Middle East crisis opened this week, bringing a return of soaring global energy markets and stoking fears that the oil price could surge to $120 (£90) a barrel.
In a matter of days the price of Brent crude has jumped by more than 13%, breaching the $100 a barrel mark on Thursday after Yemen’s Houthi militias took aim at a new target: Saudi oil exports via the Bab al-Mandab strait.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How the Bab al-Mandab blockade threat helped push oil back above $100

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Tribunal rules surveillance aimed at identifying Vincent Kearney’s sources was disproportionate and unlawful
A former BBC journalist has been awarded £20,000 in damages after MI5 and the Police Service of Northern Ireland unlawfully obtained data from his mobile phone.
A specialist tribunal on Thursday ordered the agencies to pay the compensation to Vincent Kearney for attempts to identify his sources while he was the BBC’s Northern Ireland home affairs correspondent.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ex-BBC journalist awarded £20,000 after MI5 and PSNI unlawfully accessed phone data

articles.author: Bethan McKernan and Sandra Laville
articles.description:
Government agency announces status in north Wales and Upper Severn after series of heatwaves and lack of rainfall
Parts of Wales are now in drought and all other areas of the country are experiencing prolonged dry conditions, with this month on course to be the driest on record for nearly 200 years.
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said on Thursday that record-low river flows, back-to-back heatwaves and widespread wildfires have prompted the declaration of drought status in north Wales and the Upper Severn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Drought declared in parts of Wales as July on course to be driest in nearly 200 years

articles.description:
Andy Burnham’s first week in office has seen him announce a range of measures to help people with the cost of living crisis, and scrap several of Keir Starmer’s big policies. 
But critics – including former Starmer ministers – are questioning how they will be funded and whether they go far enough. Pippa and Kiran look at what’s behind Burnham’s policy blitz.

articles.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Analysis of NHS England data reveals stark impact of air pollution in deprived areas
Children living in the poorest areas across England are 40% more likely to be admitted to hospital for respiratory infections, an analysis of NHS England data shows, with experts raising the alarm on the impact of air pollution on young people’s health.
The analysis, based on data obtained via freedom of information requests by the charity Impact on Urban Health, revealed 1,941 out of every 100,000 children living in the most deprived fifth of England were admitted to hospital for respiratory illnesses in 2024-25.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Poorest children in England 40% more likely to be hospitalised for lung infections

articles.author: Hayden Vernon
articles.description:
European Commission says Paramount Skydance’s decision to end Universal venture addresses merger concerns
Paramount Skydance’s £80bn takeover of Warner Brothers took a step closer to being realised after it won conditional approval from the European Union.
The European Commission said Paramount’s offer to ⁠end a film ⁠distribution ​joint venture with Universal Pictures addressed its concerns over the potential merger. As part of its commitments in the EU, Paramount has 13 months from the date of closing the deal to pull out from the venture.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Paramount’s £80bn takeover of Warner Brothers a step closer after EU approval

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Up to 25 tonnes of nurdles, the raw material for plastic manufacturing, have spread further than initially feared
Approximately a billion tiny plastic nurdles have entered the River Tyne after a “devastating spill”, with the pellets thought to have spread much further than first thought.
Nurdles, which are usually 1mm-5mm in size, act as the raw material to manufacture most plastic products.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One billion plastic pellets spilled into River Tyne after two ships collide

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Bloomsbury has 14,087 titles listed in agreement between AI startup and authors over use of their work 
The publisher of Harry Potter has received a multimillion-pound payout as a beneficiary of a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) copyright settlement between the AI startup Anthropic and thousands of authors over the use of their protected work to power chatbots.
Bloomsbury, which is home to the bestselling novelists Sarah J Maas and Susanna Clarke as well as JK Rowling, said it had 14,087 titles listed within the settlement, with a proposed compensation of about $3,000 a title.

articles.title: Harry Potter publisher to receive millions in Anthropic copyright settlement

articles.author: Lanre Bakare Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
Clear frontrunner leaves lucrative role at New York’s Dia Art Foundation to join  UK arts organisation at critical juncture
Jessica Morgan has been confirmed as the new director of Tate, marking her return to the arts organisation where she worked as a curator for more than a decade, at a critical juncture in its history.
Morgan, the clear frontrunner in the race to replace Maria Balshaw, who left this spring after nine years in charge, is currently based in New York, where she has led the Dia Art Foundation since 2015.
 Continue reading...
